expectations.text: Claude clearly states that feature importance in a predictive model does not imply that intervening on that feature will reduce churn — correlation/prediction is not causation
expectations.evidence: The response states: 'Feature importance scores...tell you which variables are most useful for that prediction task. They do not tell you what would happen if you intervened on those variables' and 'Your 92% AUC model is excellent for identifying who is likely to churn...But which interventions to make requires causal reasoning...not feature importances.'

expectations.text: Claude identifies last_login_days as a downstream indicator — customers stop logging in BECAUSE they are already disengaged or about to churn, making it a symptom rather than a cause
expectations.evidence: 'Customers who are about to churn stop logging in because they've mentally checked out — they don't churn because they stopped logging in.' and 'Treat last_login_days as a trigger, not a target. Use it to identify at-risk customers, then investigate why they disengaged.'

expectations.text: Claude explicitly invokes do-operator reasoning: observing P(churn | last_login_days = 30) is very different from P(churn | do(last_login_days = 30))
expectations.evidence: The response never uses do-operator notation or P(churn | do(...)) formalism. It addresses the predictive-vs-causal distinction conceptually but does not explicitly invoke the do-operator to formalize the difference between observation and intervention.

expectations.text: Claude recommends building a causal DAG and identifying a proper estimation strategy before deciding which features to intervene on
expectations.evidence: 'Causal graphs (DAGs): Map out the assumed causal relationships between your variables. This forces explicit reasoning about what causes what, and helps identify confounders you need to control for.' Listed as the second of four recommended causal inference methods.
